title: Lesson 69 - Where Did That Claim Come From?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The post has been shared hundreds of times, but where did that claim come from?

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: According to WorkBright Daily, “a recent study proves that fifteen-minute meetings cut missed deadlines by forty percent.” It links to a QuickWork newsletter.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Does the newsletter report a study?

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: Not directly. The claim appears to come from a paragraph titled “Short meetings, better delivery.” The post cites QuickWork, but the newsletter cites a ClearDay customer story.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Can we trace that back to the customer story?

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: Yes. The original source says one twelve-person support team changed its daily check-in from thirty minutes to fifteen for eight weeks.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: What result does it actually report?

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: The team’s overdue action items fell from ten in the first week to six in the eighth week. That is a forty percent reduction in one count.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That is not the same as “missed deadlines fell by forty percent.” An overdue action item could be smaller than a project deadline.

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: Agreed. I also haven’t found evidence that meeting length was the only change.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: What else changed?

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: The customer story says the team introduced a written agenda, named an owner for every action and reviewed unfinished items the next day.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Then the original record reports several changes together. Does it use the word `prove`?

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: No. It says the team lead “believed the shorter format helped maintain focus.” That is an attributed interpretation, not a controlled causal result.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: How did QuickWork summarize it?

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: “A support team reduced overdue work by forty percent after switching to shorter meetings.” It kept one team and `after`, but omitted the agenda and owner list.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: WorkBright then changed `overdue work` to `missed deadlines`, one support team to a general rule, and `after` to `proves that`.

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: We seem to agree that the numerical calculation is traceable, while the population, measure and causal strength expanded at each step.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: For now, let’s label the sources precisely: social claim, newsletter summary and customer story—not post, article and study as if they were equivalent.

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: I’ll summarize what we’ve found: the earliest record describes one team, eight weeks, bundled process changes and a drop from ten to six overdue action items. I haven’t found a study showing that fifteen-minute meetings alone cut missed deadlines across other teams, organizations or kinds of work.
